def: Net operating income divided by price. A $3,000,000 building with $150,000 NOI trades at a 5.0% cap. Lower cap rate means a higher price for the same income.
Gross income (rent plus other income, less vacancy and credit loss) minus operating expenses. Excludes debt service, depreciation, and capital expenditures.
Price divided by annual gross scheduled rent. Common shorthand for small apartment buildings where expense data is unreliable. A $2,400,000 price on $160,000 of rent is a 15.0 GRM.
Sale price divided by the number of units. The most-quoted pricing metric for multifamily, alongside price per square foot.

The gap between in-place rents and current market rents. Long-held, rent-capped buildings often carry large loss-to-lease, which buyers value as upside but can only capture at turnover or within allowed increases.
Incentives such as free rent or reduced deposits used to lease units. Effective rent is face rent minus the value of concessions spread across the lease term.
A strategy of buying underperforming property, renovating or repositioning it, and raising rents or cutting expenses to increase NOI and value.
Informal quality tiers. Class A is newer, amenitized product; Class B is older but well kept; Class C is older stock, often pre-1980, with deferred maintenance and lower rents.
Allocating a master-metered utility bill to tenants by formula (unit size, occupants). California regulates how it is disclosed and billed.
NOI divided by annual debt service. Lenders typically require 1.20x to 1.35x on multifamily; at high rates, DSCR rather than LTV often caps the loan size.
Loan amount divided by property value. Multifamily lenders commonly cap at 55% to 75% depending on lender type and coverage.
Loans sold to or guaranteed by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. Small balance programs serve 5+ unit properties with fixed-rate terms and prepayment structures.
Prepayment penalty structures. Yield maintenance compensates the lender for lost interest; a step-down declines on a schedule (e.g., 5-4-3-2-1%). Both shape when owners can sell.
The gap between what sellers ask and what buyers will pay. A wide spread means low transaction volume until one side moves.
A buyer renegotiating price or terms after going into contract, usually citing inspection findings. Retrade history is a key factor in choosing among offers.
A tax-deferred swap of investment real estate under IRC Section 1031. The investor must identify replacement property within 45 days and close within 180 days, using a qualified intermediary.
A passive, fractional ownership vehicle that qualifies as like-kind replacement property for a 1031 exchange. Popular with owners who want to stop managing property.
Contributing property to a REIT's operating partnership in exchange for OP units under IRC Section 721, deferring gain. Often a later step after a DST.
Gain attributable to depreciation taken, taxed at up to 25% federally (unrecaptured Section 1250 gain) when the property is sold rather than exchanged.
At death, inherited property's tax basis resets to fair market value, erasing deferred gain and recapture. A major reason older owners hold rather than sell.
An engineering study that reclassifies parts of a building into shorter depreciation lives (5, 7, 15 years), accelerating deductions, especially when bonus depreciation applies.
California's 1978 property tax limit: base tax of 1% of assessed value, with assessed value rising no more than 2% a year until a change in ownership triggers reassessment.

The 2020 measure that narrowed the parent-child reassessment exclusion (from February 16, 2021, it applies mainly to a family home that the child uses as a primary residence) and expanded base-year transfers for older and disabled homeowners. Rental property passed to children is generally reassessed.
A tax on recorded transfers of real property. Ventura County's rate is $1.10 per $1,000 of value; some California cities add their own.

California's 2019 statewide rent cap and just-cause law: annual increases limited to 5% plus regional CPI, never more than 10%, with exemptions such as buildings less than 15 years old and qualifying single-family homes and condos with proper notice. Currently set to sunset January 1, 2030.

A rule that a landlord may end a tenancy only for listed at-fault reasons (nonpayment, breach, nuisance) or no-fault reasons (owner move-in, withdrawal from market, substantial remodel), with relocation pay for no-fault terminations.
A 2023 law, effective April 1, 2024, that tightened AB 1482's no-fault just-cause terminations, especially substantial remodel and owner move-in, and added penalties for violations.

A 1995 state law that bars local rent control on single-family homes, condos, and buildings first occupied after February 1, 1995, and requires vacancy decontrol (rents reset to market when a unit turns over).
A 1985 state law letting owners exit the rental business by withdrawing all units from the market, subject to notice, relocation, and re-rental restrictions.
Since July 1, 2024, most California landlords may collect no more than one month's rent as a security deposit. Small landlords meeting the statute's ownership limits may collect two months.
California's balcony law requiring periodic inspection of exterior elevated elements (balconies, decks, stairways) on buildings with three or more units.
California's Fair Employment and Housing Act, which bars housing discrimination on protected characteristics, including source of income (housing vouchers).

Regional Housing Needs Allocation. The state assigns each city a number of homes to plan for by income level for each eight-year housing element cycle. Ventura County is in the SCAG region's 6th cycle (2021–2029).
The part of each city's general plan that shows how it will accommodate its RHNA, including sites rezoned for housing. It must be certified by the state housing department (HCD).
A state Housing Accountability Act provision that limits a city's ability to deny qualifying housing projects while its housing element is out of compliance.
State law granting extra units, plus concessions and waivers, to projects that include affordable housing.
A 2021 law allowing lot splits and up to two units per lot on most single-family parcels, ministerially.
Streamlined, ministerial approval for qualifying multifamily projects in jurisdictions behind on their RHNA. SB 423 extended and expanded SB 35.

Accessory dwelling unit / junior accessory dwelling unit. State law requires cities to allow ADUs ministerially, including on existing multifamily lots, where garages, storage areas, and detached space can be converted or added.

Save Open-Space and Agricultural Resources: voter initiatives first passed in 1998 and renewed in 2016 through 2050. They require a public vote to convert farmland or open space to urban uses in the county and most of its cities.
City Urban Restriction Boundary: each SOAR city's voter-approved urban growth line. Development outside it generally needs a public vote.
Land within the California Coastal Act's boundary, where development needs a coastal development permit from the city (under a certified Local Coastal Program) or the Coastal Commission.
CAL FIRE's maps rating wildfire hazard as moderate, high, or very high. The maps drive building standards, disclosures, and insurance underwriting.
California's insurer of last resort, offering basic fire coverage when the standard market will not. It is often paired with a 'difference in conditions' policy for other perils.
Buildings with a weak ground floor, typically tuck-under parking, that are vulnerable to earthquake collapse. Some California cities mandate retrofits.
Low-Income Housing Tax Credit. The main federal subsidy for affordable rental housing, awarded in California by CTCAC and requiring long-term income and rent restrictions.
A federal rent subsidy administered by local housing authorities. Tenants pay about 30% of income and the voucher covers the rest, up to the payment standard.
A tax-free housing allowance paid to service members, set by ZIP code, rank, and dependency status. It shapes rents near Naval Base Ventura County.
The City of Los Angeles transfer tax adopted in 2022 that adds a surcharge on sales above roughly $5 million. It has pushed some LA capital toward Ventura County.
A broker's written estimate of a property's market value, based on rent roll, expenses, and comparable sales. It is the standard first deliverable to a prospective seller.
